title: Student Motivation Problems Crush the Kids, and They Crush Us, Too!
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart argues that student motivation, though it sounds dull, is the problem sitting behind a teacher's daily problems, because when kids will not do work with care, education breaks down. He traces a chain: passive students master nothing, unmotivated students frustrate teachers, frustrated teachers either quit in spirit or respond with unsustainable 80-hour weeks, and the best people burn out. He presents the five key beliefs of credibility, value, belonging, effort and efficacy as the core of motivation, each tied to supporting research such as Carol Dweck's work on mindset. He anticipates the objection that this is another item for an overflowing plate and replies that once he cohered his thinking around the five beliefs, they changed the plate permanently. The post ends by tying behaviour, turn-in rates and grade-mongering across his class periods to the same roots, and invites readers to share their own reasons for studying motivation.
points: Stuart defines quitting broadly to include mental disengagement such as 'that kid's not teachable', not only resignation, which widens the burnout conversation.
He draws a causal chain from unmotivated students to frustrated teachers to either quitting or overwork, to show motivation as a retention issue.
He recasts the five key beliefs as short statements students would say to themselves, such as 'My teacher is good at her job' and 'I can succeed at this'.
He argues that motivation is not another item on the plate but a lens that explains behaviour problems, low turn-in rates and grade-mongering across different hours.
He claims the approach is sustainable because results improve without crushing a teacher's family or health under overwork.
quotes: But here's the thing: when kids aren’t motivated to do work with care, the whole endeavor of education breaks down. - You can’t passively master anything, except passivity. For our kids to master art and science and mathematics and history, they’ve got to do work. And for that work to have its maximum impact, it’s got to be done with attention and focus and curiosity and engagement.

When teachers are faced with unmotivated kids, they get frustrated. One of the most painful things for an educator’s heart is to put work into lesson planning or paper grading or relationship building or curriculum mapping, only to find that their efforts are met with apathy or silliness or grade-mongering or complaint.

When teachers get frustrated, they quit — either fully or partially. I define quitting broadly. It’s not just when you put in your letter of resignation. It’s when you say, “Eh, yeah, that kid’s not teachable.” Or “Her home life is too rough.” Or “Whatever, it just is what it is — you can lead a horse to water, right?” When you quit, you stop growing.

Or sometimes, teachers respond to frustration with unsustainable overwork. This is what happens to many of our best people. They meet problems stemming from student motivation issues, and they respond with 80-hour weeks. Within a few years, they’re gone — used up like tissues.

When this is happening in my class, I look like a better teacher and feel like a better teacher and get results like a better teacher. And the best thing is that it's all sustainable — I’m not crushing my family or my health beneath the burden of overwork.

Value says, “This work matters to me.” Do you know many kids who are motivated by work that they view as totally pointless? Me neither. I know few adults like that, either. But when they do value the work, it’s so much easier for them to do. And the value belief is highly malleable at the classroom level.

But listen: student motivation is the problem behind our daily problems. The behavior issues in sixth hour, the low turn-in rates in fifth hour, the poor achievement in second, the grade-mongering in first — these all have the same roots.
